Senses.Note: Primary family check: 'visible form/color' (色), 'sound' (聲), 'seeing and hearing' (見聞), 'sound, form, and language' (聲色言語), and 'sound, form, and names' (聲色名字). The ordinary 'sensual attractions' and the idiom 'without changing voice or expression' refer to different things and are split below under depth-gate item 8. Senses.Explanation: The paired sensory objects of ear and eye: sound (聲) and visible form or color (色). Chan records do more than repeat the pair abstractly. Yongjia's exchange explicitly assigns them to the faculties — 'when eyes and ears meet sound and form' (眼耳緣聲色時) — and asks what is the substance of sound and form. Dahui makes the pair demonstrable during a public address: he raises the whisk and says, 'this is form,' strikes the Chan seat and says, 'this is sound' (這箇是色／這箇是聲). Another record gives ordinary audible examples: wind in pine trees, frogs, and crows are all sound, while saying that what one discriminates is sound and form. The corpus also predicates 'pass through all sound and form without obstruction' (透一切聲色，無有滯礙) and draws its own distinction between function 'together with sound and form' and 'the affairs of sound and form' (用同聲色而不是聲色之事). The Zen deviation is this repeated use as a named field of public testing and concrete demonstration; the graphs still denote what is heard and seen.

Senses.Note: The phrase 'cast off sensual attractions' (擯去聲色) occurs in nine allowlist texts, chiefly recensions of the same Zhao Bian biography; 'indulge in sensual attractions' (耽聲色) supplies a structurally independent witness. No distinctively Chan lexical bend was found for this ordinary sense. Frozen-corpus concordance: 2545 exact hits in 339 storage files representing 334 independent works.

Occurrences.Kwic: 非一面作功名、受富貴、耽聲色、料理世情，一面又去學可以了得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J20/J20nB098.xml). Further Questions to Chan Master Huangbo Wunian (黃蘗無念禪師復問): Huangbo Wunian Shenyou owns the exact clause in the complete case.

Senses.Explanation: A distinct ordinary referent in biographical and admonitory prose: worldly sensual attractions or entertainments, commonly coordinated with wealth, status, and profit. Zhao Bian's biography says that after forty he 'cast off sensual attractions' (擯去聲色) and turned his attention to the records of the school. Another record warns against simultaneously pursuing achievement, receiving wealth and honor, 'indulging in sensual attractions' (耽聲色), and attending to worldly affairs. This is not the eye-and-ear field concretely demonstrated by a whisk and struck seat, so it remains a separate sense.

Senses.Note: Kept separate because a person's voice and expression and the field of heard and seen objects cannot share one precise English gloss. Frozen-corpus concordance: 2545 exact hits in 339 storage files representing 334 independent works.

Senses.Explanation: The two outward signs in the fixed phrase 'without changing voice or expression' (不動聲色): voice or tone (聲) and facial look or demeanor (色). A record praises Huanglong's forty years presiding over a community as 'holding the seat of the community without changing voice or expression' (坐鎮道場，不動聲色); a public interview likewise asks whether something can be discerned 'without changing voice or expression.' This idiomatic human demeanor is a different referent from sounds and visible objects in the sensory field.
